transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-11
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Derek Patel (Redwood SE), Jonas Vega (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (AmbLab), Luis Gomez (AmbLab SRE), Erin Park (AmbLab CTO), Samir Khan (Product)

Summary (auto):
Quick scoping for a reserved GPU POC with burst capacity/fallbacks. Discussed success criteria (latency SLOs, cost targets, model fidelity), workload shape, benchmark plan, timeline and responsibilities. Agreed to run 48h reserved+burst benchmark and share security docs.

Topics (auto):
- Success criteria & SLAs
- Reserved capacity sizing and burst credits
- Fallback model variants and routing
- KV cache and batching expectations
- Security/VPC/KMS constraints
- Benchmark plan and timeline

Action items (auto):
See metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Thanks everyone for joining, appreciate you carving time. Quick intro, I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, and Derek is our SE who will lead the POC bench. Jonas is also on the call to help with the onboarding bits. Priya, do you want to kick off with current stack and goals?
[00:18] Priya (Amberstone): Yeah sure, thanks Maya. So Amberstone is building a real-time summarization pipeline for analyst notes, this is pretty latency sensitive, target 95th <= 300 ms for short docs, but for longer sessions we can tolerate up to 800 ms. Our main worry is making this predictable at scale and not exploding cost.
[00:34] Erin (CTO): Also, security — all inference must go through our VPC, keys via our KMS, and we need audit logs retained for 1 year. SOC2 is obvious, and SAML SSO for console.
[00:47] Derek (SE): Got it. That matches a lot of customers. On the POC side we usually do reserved capacity sized to your steady-state QPS and then a burst strategy for spikes. Quick question — what's your steady-state tokens/sec or requests/sec?
[01:02] Priya: Right now our staging traces show a steady 45 rps with 2-3 second average documents; peak bursts up to 220 rps during morning ingest. The distribution is spiky — roughly 8% of minutes are high-burst.
[01:18] Jonas (SE): Good. For sizing reserved GPUs we usually map expected throughput to tokens/sec per GPU given the model variant. Which model are you planning?
[01:26] Samir (Product): We're evaluating a 13B open model we finetuned, currently running fp16 on our infra. Curious about quantization options if that helps cost.
[01:36] Derek: Perfect. For a 13B with A100-like perf, ballpark is 8–12 rps per GPU for the end-to-end latency target you mentioned, depends on batching and sequence length. With Redwood's continuous batching and prefix cache you often see 2–3x improvement, so planning reserved to cover 45 steady rps would be 4–6 GPUs reserved. Then we recommend burst credits (or autoscale) to reach up to 220 rps — that means allowing up to additional 14 GPUs for short periods, with graceful fallback to a quantized variant first.
[02:01] Luis (SRE): Sorry, can you repeat the fallback sequence? We prefer deterministic behavior: if reserved capacity exhausted then first try quantized 13B, then route to smaller 7B, then queue with a priority window.
[02:15] Derek: Yes, our recommendation matches that pattern. Fallback order we typically configure: 1) Same model in int8/4 quantized mode on same GPU type (lower perf hit, big cost savings), 2) Model variant (7B) compatible with same prompt, 3) Queue with a short TTL and graceful 429+retry with backoff, 4) If region capacity exhausted then cross-region failover to secondary region — only if your data residency allows.
[02:36] Priya: Cross-region is tricky for us, prefer to keep within EU region. We'll likely need queueing before cross-region.
[02:42] Maya: Noted. We'll set the routing policy to prefer same-region fallbacks and avoid cross-region unless explicitly allowed.
[02:50] Erin: On the security front — can you detail the Private deployment vs Dedicated for POC? We want customer-managed VPC and KMS, but not full on-prem.
[03:02] Jonas: Dedicated reserved nodes can live inside your VPC via Private mode VPN peering — you keep KMS keys and audit logs; Redwood control plane can be configured to not store payloads. For the POC we can do a semi-private setup: dedicated reserved GPUs in a customer VPC with a private control plane tunnel. That meets audit and KMS needs without shipping on-prem software.
[03:22] Luis: What about egress and company firewall rules? We have strict egress policy, no outbound to uncontrolled IPs.
[03:29] Derek: We provide known outbound ranges and a peered endpoint; we can also deploy a NAT gateway on your side. We'll share a networking spec.
[03:36] Priya: Good. And the benchmark — we want metrics: p95 latency, p99 latency, cost per 1M tokens, failure rate, model output quality delta vs our baseline.
[03:46] Maya: We'll capture those. Derek, can you run through the benchmark plan?
[03:50] Derek: Sure. Proposed 48-hour run broken into: 24h steady-state (45 rps) on reserved capacity, 8h simulated spikes matching production histogram (including back-to-back minute-level spikes to exercise autoscale and burst), and a 16h mixed phase to verify fallback ordering and cache hit behavior. We'll collect throughput/tokens/sec, per-request latency, queueing times, model variant routing, and cost burn. We'll also run a small qualitative eval set against your current finetuned model to catch regressions; if we see >3% generation quality drop on key metrics, we treat as a failure point.
[04:21] Priya: For quality we measure rouge-l and a human rating on 200 sampled outputs. Can you accomodate human eval integration?
[04:28] Derek: Yes we can include that. We'll export outputs to a secure bucket you control.
[04:32] Erin: Timeline — what's realistic to start the benchmark? Our infra team can provision a test VPC but need a week lead.
[04:38] Maya: If we get your sample payloads and VPC details by next Friday (2027-08-14), we can provision reserved capacity and start the bench on Wed 2027-08-18. That aligns with the action items we captured.
[04:48] Luis: What's the expected cost model for the POC? We need a firm estimate for reserved hours + expected burst credit consumption.
[04:55] Maya: We'll send an estimated cost sheet. For the sizes we discussed — 4–6 reserved GPUs for steady-state plus burst window for up to ~14 extra GPUs — we can show two scenarios: conservative burst usage (2–3 hours/day) and worst-case (10 hours/day). We'll include options for billing reserved monthly vs hourly for the POC term.
[05:12] Priya: Do you support preemptible/spot for burst? We have tolerance for some retries on large spikes.
[05:18] Derek: Yes, spot-backed burst pools are an option; they'll have higher failure rates but much lower cost. We can configure mixed pools: prefer on-demand for critical routes, fall back to spot for lower-priority traffic.
[05:29] Samir: A question about metrics and observability — can we get token-level cost and tracing into our APM?
[05:35] Jonas: We have token-level cost and can push traces via OTLP to your collector. We'll add per-route dashboards and alerts.
[05:42] Luis: For the fallback queue TTL, we want max 10s for high-priority requests, otherwise reject. Can Redwood do prioritized queues?
[05:49] Derek: Yes, we support multi-priority queues and rate-limited retry windows. We'll show configuration examples in the runbook.
[05:56] Priya: Also curious about KV cache — our workload re-uses prefixes a lot. How effective is prefix caching across requests?
[06:03] Derek: With repeated prefixes you'll see big benefits. Our runtime does KV cache sharing per customer and per model variant; depending on reuse you can see token reduction up to 40% for those flows. We'll instrument cache hit rate during the benchmark.
[06:16] Erin: Any blockers on data residency? We need EU-only processing for production. For POC we can do EU region, but cross-region fallback must be off.
[06:24] Maya: We'll mark cross-region failover disabled for the POC. The fallback policy will keep everything in the EU region.
[06:29] Priya: For acceptance criteria — we propose: p95 <= 300 ms for short docs, p95 <= 800 ms for long docs, failure rate < 0.5%, cost not exceeding 1.4x our current infra spend for same throughput, and no regressions >3% on core quality metrics.
[06:46] Maya: That sounds like a clear set of criteria. We'll formalize and include in the POC SOW.
[06:51] Derek: I'll also include a contingency: if reserved capacity can't be met in-region we will simulate equivalent capacity locally for bench results but mark it as simulated.
[06:59] Luis: One last infra question — do you support customer-managed KMS and per-tenant encryption keys?
[07:06] Jonas: Yes, we support KMS integrations and per-tenant CMEK. We'll include steps for key rotation and audit log access in the security doc.
[07:13] Maya: Great. Recap on next steps: Maya shares POC deck and security docs by Friday; Derek shares benchmark plan and metrics; Priya and Luis share payloads and VPC/KMS details; schedule 48h run for Wed the 18th.
[07:28] Priya: Sounds good. One ask — can you also provide a short runbook for on-call play for the POC? We want to know who to loop in during an incident.
[07:36] Maya: Yes we'll send an on-call play and the escalation matrix.
[07:39] Erin: Thanks all.
[07:41] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with the deck and action items.
[07:46] (call ends)
